value.produces: assets/multics/{bin/dps8,media/{root.dsk,12.8MULTICS.tap},rootfs} — the DPS8M R3.1.0 simulator, the MR12.8 QuickStart RPV baked past the forced password change and SHUT DOWN CLEAN, the MR12.8 system tape, and the container rootfs (relaunch reset)

labctl.notes: EMULATED MACHINE, CONTAINED, NO CHECKPOINT: the DPS8M simulator runs Multics MR12.8 on an emulated DPS-8/M inside a systemd-nspawn container together with the station's Xvfb and one xterm; the daemon captures the X root (SH_CAPTURE=x11) and types over XTEST (SH_INPUT_BACKEND=x11test). There is no pointer — this is a terminal exhibit. No QMP and no exec channel: `labctl shot` reads the X root. The visitor line is FNP D channel d.h000 on the CONTAINER's loopback port 6180, so it is unreachable from labhost; to drive the guest by hand, enter the container's netns — `nsenter -t $(cat /data/vms/streamhost/stations/multics/mame.pid) -n telnet 127.0.0.1 6180` — and only while no visitor is attached. mame.pid is the DPS8M `dps8` HOST pid (idle freezer and reap-by-exe), nspawn.pid the supervisor. The operator console is NOT the museum surface: it goes to work/emulator.log and carries the `M-> ` attention prompt and BCE. Reset=relaunch: kill dps8 by mame.pid, wipe work/, reflink-copy the pristine baked RPV back and start again (~60 s to the login banner; the copy itself is 0.126 s for 594 MB). Launcher stations/multics/x11-runtime.sh, which execs the lane's shared engine docs/lab/record-wave/shared-terminal-runtime.sh; assets in assets/multics (MANIFEST.sha256 pins them).

pointer.device: none — a 1969 timesharing terminal has no pointing device, and the FNP line carries keystrokes only. The x11test backend is present for KEYS only (SH_X11TEST_KEYS=1).

museum.lineage: CTSS (MIT, 1961) → Multics (MIT Project MAC + Bell Labs + General Electric, designed 1964, in service 1969) → Honeywell and then Bull; and, by way of Bell Labs walking out in 1969, Unix — whose name is a joke at this system's expense
museum.arch: Honeywell DPS-8/M — the last machine Multics ran on: a 36-bit word, segmented and paged, with eight hardware protection rings and a Front-End Network Processor (an FNP: a minicomputer whose whole job is the terminal lines) carrying the visitor's terminal on channel d.h000
eraSoftware: Multics Emacs — Bernard Greenberg's 1978 display editor, written in Lisp, the ancestor of every extensible Emacs since
qedx and ted, the line editors
runoff and compose, the text formatters
the Multics PL/I compiler — the system is written in it
FORTRAN, BASIC, APL, Lisp, Pascal and C

museum.periodBrowser: none — Multics predates the web by twenty years; its network was the ARPANET, and this exhibit is deliberately not networked at all
museum.blurb: The most influential operating system almost nobody used. Multics was designed in 1964 by MIT, Bell Labs and General Electric to sell computing the way a utility sells electricity, and it went into service in 1969 with a list of ideas that took the rest of the industry thirty years to finish copying: a hierarchical file system with a root and symbolic links, access control lists, dynamic linking at first reference, a shell that is an ordinary replaceable program, and a single-level store in which a file is simply a piece of memory you address. It was written in PL/I rather than assembler, which everyone said was impossible. Bell Labs quit the project in 1969 and two of its engineers went off to write something smaller, named as a pun on the thing they had left. Around eighty Multics sites were ever sold; the last one, at the Canadian Department of National Defence, was shut down in October 2000. Bull released the source in 2007, and this is that source, running on a simulated DPS-8/M.
museum.notes: Tier 3, EMULATED but CONTAINED and with no checkpoint: the DPS8M simulator (R3.1.0), the station's Xvfb and the visitor's xterm all run inside one systemd-nspawn container (private PID/mount/net/IPC/UTS/user namespaces, uid base 2555904, volatile overlay root, assets bound read-only, CAP_SYS_ADMIN dropped). The visitor surface is one 80x24 xterm on FNP channel d.h000; the operator console — the `M-> ` attention prompt and BCE — is never on screen. The released MR12.8 QuickStart forces a password change on the first login, which no visitor should ever be shown, so the exhibit's RPV is baked once with that change already made and then shut down cleanly. No checkpoint: reset is a relaunch from that pristine RPV, reflink-copied in 0.126 s. See docs/guests/multics.md.

emulator.source: dps8m.gitlab.io R3.1.0 linux-64 release (statically linked); Multics MR12.8 from the community QuickStart release. Both hashed in assets/multics/MANIFEST.sha256 and staged by scripts/build-guests/tiles/multics.sh

network.note: No network plane and no retronet. Multics had ARPANET networking but the FNP terminal line is the whole visitor surface here, and the station is an island on purpose. The FNP telnet listener lives on the container's own loopback behind --private-network, so it claims no host port and is unreachable from labhost.

reset.mouse: N/A — no pointing device. A Multics FNP line carries keystrokes only, and the exhibit publishes no pointer (stream.pointer.present=false).

notes: Record wave 2026-09-20, Lane B (docs/lab/MULTICS-WAVE.md). This station contributed findings 1, 2 and 4 to the lane's shared heritage-terminal runtime (docs/lab/record-wave/shared-terminal-runtime.sh, proven end to end by vax43bsd): a TCP port probe is not readiness (port at +4 s, answering service at +52 s), never give the hidden emulator a pipe or a FIFO on stdin, and an operator console driven by an attention key must handshake on a NEW prompt.
